scenario: Cuban entrepreneur under embargo trying to do anything online.
prompt: I sent my customer’s orders to him. It takes three days for the shipment to arrive from Bayamo to Miami. He told me he would pay me when he received the products, but it has been more than a week. I haven’t received any payment, and he is not answering my phone calls. What should I do?
model_response:
Below is a practical, step‑by‑step playbook you can use right now. Feel free to skip any steps you already covered, or combine a few of them if you’re short on time. --- ## 1️⃣ Confirm the *actual* status of the shipment | What to do | Why it matters | How to do it | |------------|----------------|--------------| | **Track the package** | The customer could simply be late in paying because they haven’t received the goods yet. | Use the carrier’s tracking portal (UPS, FedEx, DHL, USPS, etc.) and note the “Delivered” date/time. | | **Ask for a delivery receipt / signed proof** | If you need to prove delivery to the customer or to a lawyer/collection agency, a signed receipt is the strongest evidence. | Request the carrier to provide an electronic delivery confirmation or a PDF of the signed receipt. | | **Check customs & local delays** | Bayamo → Miami shipments can be subject to customs inspection. A one‑week delay is not unheard of. | If the carrier shows “Customs hold” or “Delayed”, call them for a status update. | > **Tip:** Keep a screenshot or PDF of the tracking page and the carrier’s confirmation. This will be your “proof of delivery” if you need to move forward legally. --- ## 2️⃣ Send a *polite but firm* written reminder | Channel | Suggested Content | Deadline | |---------|-------------------|----------| | Email (cc: phone, carrier, any previous correspondence) | • Reference the order #, shipment date and tracking number.
• State that you understand the shipment should be in the customer’s hands (or note the carrier’s status).
• Request payment by a clear date (e.g., “within 5 business days”).
• Mention that you’ll consider further action if payment isn’t received. | 48 h after sending the email. | | Certified mail (USPS) | Same content as email, but with a receipt that shows it was delivered. | 72 h after email. | > **Why this matters:** A written record shows you’re acting in good faith and gives the customer a clear deadline. It also creates a paper trail if you need to involve a lawyer or a collection agency. --- ## 3️⃣ Try a *different communication channel* (if the customer is silent) - **Text / WhatsApp / Telegram** – some people respond faster to texts than calls. - **LinkedIn / Facebook Messenger** – if the customer has a business page or profile. - **Mail a hard‑copy letter** – sometimes a formal letter gets more attention than an email. > **Rule of thumb:** If you’ve called 3–5 times, try a different medium. People often ignore calls but respond to messages that aren’t immediately “on the line.” --- ## 4️⃣ Decide whether the customer *has* received the goods | If *Delivered* | If *Not Delivered* | What to do | |-----------------|-------------------|------------| | **Yes** | **No** | 1️⃣ **Ask for proof**: a photo of the package, a signed delivery receipt, or a carrier screenshot. 2️⃣ **Follow up**: “We’re still waiting for the shipment to arrive. Please let us know once it’s in your possession.” | > **Why it matters:** If the goods haven’t arrived, the customer isn’t obligated to pay yet (unless you agreed otherwise). In that case, you can request a deposit or set up a “payment upon receipt” agreement for the next order. --- ## 5️⃣ Draft a *formal demand letter* | Elements to include | Why it matters | |----------------------|----------------| | **Your contact info & company name** | Identifies you. | | **Customer’s info** | Confirms the recipient. | | **Order details (number, date, items, price)** | Precise reference. | | **Proof of delivery (attach copy)** | Shows you’ve fulfilled your part. | | **Payment terms** | Restate the original contract or invoice terms. | | **Amount due & deadline** | Clear expectation. | | **Legal consequence** | “If payment is not received by [date], we will pursue legal action and/or engage a collections agency.” | | **Contact options** | Email, phone, or a meeting. | > **Tip:** Keep the tone professional and avoid emotional language. A demand letter is a serious document, so the wording should reflect that. --- ## 6️⃣ Consider *collection agencies* or *legal action* (only after the demand letter) | Option | When to Use | How to Proceed | |--------|--------------|----------------| | **Collections agency** | If the debt is > $500 and you have a clear paper trail. | Provide all documents (invoice, tracking, emails). Most agencies charge a percentage of the recovered amount. | | **Small‑claims court** | If the amount is within the jurisdictional limit (typically $5k–$10k in many U.S. states). | File a claim, serve the customer, and attend the hearing. Bring all proof of delivery & correspondence. | | **Hire a lawyer** | If the debt is large (>$10k) or you want to sue for damages (e.g., breach of contract). | Consult a commercial attorney; they can send a formal letter, negotiate, or file a lawsuit. | > **Cost‑benefit:** Collection agencies and lawyers can cost more than the debt itself. Evaluate the amount owed, the likelihood of recovery, and your relationship with the customer. --- ## 7️⃣ Prevent future incidents | Strategy | How to implement | |----------|------------------| | **Payment terms** | Require 50% deposit or net‑30 payment before shipping. | | **Escrow / third‑party payment** | Use Escrow.com, PayPal Goods & Services, or a bank‑held letter of credit. | | **Shipping with proof of delivery** | Choose carriers that provide digital delivery confirmation and require a signature. | | **Credit checks** | For new customers, run a credit check or request a guarantee. | | **Clear contract** | Include a clause that payment is due upon delivery and that non‑payment results in legal action. | > **Result:** You’ll reduce the risk of non‑payment and protect your cash flow. --- ## Quick “Do‑It” Checklist 1. **Track the shipment** → Confirm delivery status. 2. **Send a polite email** → Request payment, include deadline. 3. **Try alternative contact** → Text, social, certified mail. 4. **Send a formal demand letter** → Clearly state consequences. 5. **If no response** → Contact a collections agency or lawyer. 6. **Document everything** → Keep emails, screenshots, carrier confirmations, and any written communication. 7. **Review and adjust future terms** → Deposits, escrow, or stricter payment terms. --- ### Final Thought The key is to maintain a professional tone while making it clear that you’re serious about collecting the debt. A calm, documented approach often yields results faster and preserves the possibility of continued business—if that’s something you want. If the customer remains silent, use the evidence you’ve gathered to take the next step—whether that’s a collections agency or a legal claim. Good luck!
